records.title: Progress in parabiotic mouse models: From origins to modern applications.
records.abstract: The parabiotic mouse model involves a surgical technique that connects the circulatory systems of two mice, enabling the sharing of peripheral circulatory system, immune cells, and various physiological factors. This review traces the historical development of the model from its initial establishment by Paul Bert in the 19th century to the present, summarizes technical improvements in surgical methods, animal adaptation, and model stability, and systematically outlines its cutting-edge applications in fields such as aging reversal, immune tolerance mechanisms, cancer biology, neuroscience, and metabolic diseases. Studies demonstrate that heterochronic parabiosis can reverse aging phenotypes in tissues of older mice and reveal the pivotal role of circulating factors in disease progression. Despite technical challenges and ethical considerations, the integration of this model with multi-omics technologies and organoid research holds promising prospects, providing essential tools for regenerative medicine and the elucidation of complex disease mechanisms. The model's irreplaceability stems from its ability to simulate systemic, whole-body physiological interactions, which cannot be fully replicated by in vitro systems like organ chips or organoids. Importantly, we provide critical synthesis of conflicting findings and highlight methodological caveats to guide future research.

records.title: Patient-Derived Organoids in Pancreatic Cancer Pharmacology: From Pharmacotyping Methodology to the AVATAR Phase III Trial and the Pharmacological Frontier.
records.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) carries a five-year survival below 13%, and most patients receive empirical first-line chemotherapy that has advanced only modestly in two decades. Pharmacological progress has been constrained by two features of the disease: a mutational landscape dominated by KRAS mutations until recently considered undruggable, and a desmoplastic stroma that obstructs both cytotoxic and immunological intervention. Patient-derived organoids (PDOs), three-dimensional cultures grown from primary or biopsy tumour tissue, have become the dominant functional platform in PDAC pharmacology, supporting drug-sensitivity profiling, combination screening, and drug-delivery evaluation in patient-matched culture. The 2025 AVATAR Phase III trial provided the first randomised evaluation of an integrated genomic, PDO, and patient-derived xenograft (PDX) personalised pharmacotherapy strategy in metastatic PDAC. It reported no intention-to-treat survival benefit (median overall survival 8.6 versus 8.7 months, p = 0.849). Of the 39 experimental-arm patients who proceeded to a second or subsequent line, 35 did not receive matched therapy, and clinical deterioration was the leading reason, recorded in 26. Yet the four patients (10%) who did receive matched therapy reached a median overall survival of 19.3 months. Because this subgroup was very small (n = 4) and non-randomised, that observation is exploratory and hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory, and it points to operational constraints as the dominant limit on clinical performance. This review synthesises the AVATAR result with the foundational pharmacotyping framework of Tiriac et al (2018), the chemoresistance and combination-pharmacology literature, and recent KRAS-inhibitor screens, clarifying what PDOs can and cannot accomplish for patients with PDAC in 2026. Pharmacological priorities for the field are addressed in detail, principally compressing the diagnostic pipeline and integrating stromal co-culture so that combination-library design rests on biologically faithful drug-response prediction.

records.title: Epithelial inflammatory memory in ulcerative colitis: molecular mechanisms and translational implications.
records.abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) can relapse after clinical and endoscopic remission, raising the question of whether previously inflamed epithelium retains altered responsiveness. Patient-derived colonic organoids and lineage-resolved colitis models show that inflammation-associated chromatin accessibility can persist after removal of the original environment and influence subsequent epithelial behavior. Basal inflammatory transcription, however, can return toward normal during organoid expansion. These observations distinguish ongoing inflammatory output from latent regulatory competence; transcriptomic normalization alone neither establishes nor excludes functional memory. Differences between paired colonic regions and persistence across molecular layers support spatial and molecular heterogeneity. Exposure history, treatment, and patient characteristics are plausible modifiers whose independent contributions remain unresolved. This Review focuses on the evidence for epithelial inflammatory memory in UC and its implications for regeneration and mucosal healing. We examine how stem and regenerative lineages could retain prior experience, with emphasis on enhancer accessibility and the supporting evidence for histone, DNA-methylation, and metabolic mechanisms. Persistent epithelial states are distinguished from continued niche stimulation, reversible adaptation, fixed injury, and somatic clonal selection. Altered recall can accelerate repair while coexisting with deficient differentiation, barrier function, or regenerative reserve, making functional recovery more informative than inflammatory output alone. Translational opportunities include targeted biopsy assays linked to organoid recall, longitudinal sampling during remission, and interventions that restore mature epithelial function. Stepwise assay validation and treatment testing could connect these mechanisms to clinical outcomes, although no epithelial memory assay or memory-directed therapy is currently validated for routine UC care.

records.title: Immune-epithelial coordination of barrier repair in inflammatory bowel disease: from cell survival to functional healing.
records.abstract: Epithelial repair in inflammatory bowel disease involves preservation of viable cells, coverage of wounds, renewal of epithelial populations and recovery of selective transport and secretion. These processes overlap, yet improvement in one does not establish completion of the others. This narrative review examines how immune signals influence these transitions and how experimental repair findings relate to patient outcomes. We first describe the junctional and mucus barrier and the distinction between physiological, endoscopic and histological measurements. We then examine epithelial death control, regenerative pathways and immune-derived signals using studies selected for compartment-specific perturbation, functional measurements or informative discrepancies between experimental and clinical findings. Interleukin-22 illustrates the importance of context: it promotes regeneration in several experimental systems, disrupts barrier function in a human colon chip, and has not yielded demonstrated efficacy as efmarodocokin alfa in a phase II ulcerative colitis trial. In one small infliximab study, paired measurements from nine patients showed an increase in epithelial resistance after treatment. Larger controlled studies are needed to establish how consistently functional recovery accompanies immune control. We organize the evidence around target engagement, epithelial response, barrier function and patient benefit, with example assays and common interpretive pitfalls for each. The resulting synthesis identifies the measurements needed to distinguish protection from repair and to test whether an epithelial effect adds value to effective immune therapy. Clinical studies must ultimately establish that a specified functional improvement is durable and beneficial to patients.

records.title: Necrotizing enterocolitis as a disorder of neonatal mucosal immune ecology: from dysbiosis and barrier failure to regulated cell death and precision prevention.
records.abstract: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) remains one of the most severe gastrointestinal emergencies of prematurity. Although survival of extremely preterm infants has improved, NEC continues to cause substantial mortality, intestinal failure, neurodevelopmental impairment, and prolonged neonatal intensive care. Its pathogenesis has traditionally been described as a convergence of prematurity, enteral feeding, intestinal ischemia, and abnormal bacterial colonization. This model remains useful, but it does not fully explain why only a subset of high-risk infants develop NEC or why single interventions show inconsistent benefit. This narrative review examines classic preterm NEC as a disorder of neonatal mucosal immune ecology, while distinguishing it from spontaneous intestinal perforation and predominantly hemodynamic injury in congenital heart disease. Epithelial immaturity, dysbiosis, altered microbial metabolism, exaggerated pattern-recognition signaling, immune-cell activation, endothelial dysfunction, thromboinflammation, and regulated cell death amplify one another. Particular attention is given to cell-specific signaling, the interaction of vascular and epithelial injury, and the distinction between protective autophagy and destructive stress responses. These mechanisms inform translational opportunities involving mother's own milk, donor human milk, strain-specific probiotics, postbiotics, defined microbial metabolites, extracellular vesicles, organoids, and multi-omics biomarkers. A mucosal immune-ecology model supports precision prevention based on developmental timing, microbial function, immune state, and injury mechanism.

records.title: A biomimetic desmoplastic pancreatic cancer organoid model reveals macrophage contributions to stiffness-associated chemoresistance.
records.abstract: In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the tumor microenvironment (TME) is characterized by a desmoplastic stroma that is markedly stiffer than normal pancreatic tissue. While increased extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffness has been shown to promote chemoresistance in tumor cells, the impact of these biophysical cues on tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) has yet to be fully explored. This gap is due in part to the lack of model systems that recapitulate both stiff environments and macrophage involvement. To address this limitation, we developed a biomimetic, three-dimensional (3D) co-culture model that integrates PDAC organoids, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), and macrophages within tunable fibrotic matrices that recapitulate the stiff ECM of the PDAC microenvironment. Using this 3D system, we demonstrate that CAF-mediated matrix remodeling drives increased stiffness and enhances chemoresistance of PDAC organoids, effects not captured in conventional two-dimensional stiffness platforms. Incorporation of macrophages into the model further amplified this protective effect, with stiff tri-culture conditions exhibiting minimal response to gemcitabine compared to organoid-CAF cultures alone. In this context, matrix stiffness and tumor-derived cues altered macrophage behavior, including reduced M1-associated marker expression. Application of the model further identified TRPV4 signaling as a contributor to stiffness-associated chemoresistance, as pharmacological inhibition of TRPV4 sensitized organoids to gemcitabine treatment within stiff tri-cultures. Together, these findings establish a biomimetic platform for investigating immune-stromal-tumor interactions within the mechanically complex PDAC microenvironment and demonstrate how CAF-driven matrix remodeling can reveal biologically relevant mechanisms of therapeutic resistance that are not apparent in simplified model systems.

records.title: FeDx-SF@βE assembly for AML treatment via GATA1/SLC40A1 pathway-mediated iron homeostasis disorder.
records.abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is an aggressive hematologic malignancy characterized by rapid progression, therapeutic resistance, and poor prognosis. Inducing ferroptosis in AML cells represents a promising therapeutic strategy. In this study, transcriptomic analyses first revealed that ferroptosis-associated transcriptional states were closely associated with prognosis and ex vivo drug-response heterogeneity in AML, providing a rationale for ferroptosis-oriented therapeutic design. Based on these findings, and further supported by a transcriptome-based target-scoring strategy, β-elemene (βE), a clinically used natural compound derived from traditional Chinese medicine, was selected as a candidate ferroptosis-related agent. We subsequently developed a nanodelivery system, designated FeDx-SF@βE, based on alcohol-induced silk fibroin (SF) folding to co-deliver ferric dextran (FeDx) and βE. The resulting nanoparticles exhibited a uniform particle size of 182.3 nm, favorable colloidal stability, and sustained drug release behavior. In vitro studies demonstrated efficient cellular uptake of FeDx-SF@βE by AML cells, leading to significantly inhibited cell viability. Pharmacological cell-death inhibitor rescue experiments showed that ferrostatin-1 produced the most pronounced protective effect, indicating that FeDx-SF@βE-induced AML cell death was predominantly ferroptosis-dependent. Mechanistically, βE-containing treatment suppressed the nuclear translocation of the transcription factor GATA1 and downregulated the iron efflux channel SLC40A1. GATA1/SLC40A1 gain- and loss-of-function analyses further demonstrated that activation of this axis attenuated FeDx-SF@βE-induced iron overload and ferroptotic injury, whereas suppression of this axis promoted intracellular iron retention, oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and mitochondrial damage. In combination with FeDx-derived iron supply, βE-mediated inhibition of the GATA1/SLC40A1 iron-export axis resulted in intracellular iron overload, glutathione depletion, ROS accumulation, extensive lipid peroxidation, and ferroptosis. Bulk transcriptomic and virtual-cell analyses further supported the involvement of the GATA1/SLC40A1 axis in ferroptosis-associated AML states and linked βE-related transcriptional programs to this regulatory mechanism. In a disseminated AML xenograft model, FeDx-SF@βE exhibited enhanced antileukemic efficacy and favorable biosafety. Collectively, this work provides a combined ferroptosis-oriented nanotherapeutic strategy for AML treatment and highlights the GATA1/SLC40A1 iron-homeostasis axis as a functionally relevant mechanism for ferroptosis-targeted nanomedicine design.

records.title: scREFINE: Label-efficient refinement of frozen scGPT embeddings for single-cell RNA-seq clustering.
records.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) clustering remains challenging because of high dimensionality, sparsity, technical noise, and limited cell annotations. Here, we propose scREFINE, a label-efficient semi-supervised clustering framework that adapts pretrained single-cell foundation-model embeddings for accurate cell clustering. scREFINE uses a lightweight refinement head to map cells into a task-specific clustering space using only 5% labeled cells, while treating the remaining cells as unlabeled during training. To exploit information from unlabeled cells, scREFINE introduces stability-aware soft structural regularization over local neighborhoods, which leverages reliable cell-cell relations as auxiliary guidance without relying on hard pseudo-label constraints. Experiments on five benchmark scRNA-seq datasets show that scREFINE achieves the best ARI on every dataset against every baseline under an identical, leakage-free protocol (mean ± SD over four seeds). A paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test over the five per-dataset means yields p=0.0625, above the conventional 0.05 threshold because only five datasets are available; we therefore interpret the consistent improvements as strong empirical evidence rather than a statistically conclusive demonstration. A common-embedding comparison confirms that these gains arise from task-specific refinement rather than the pretrained representation alone: adapted baselines receiving identical embeddings achieve 0.00-0.61 ARI, compared with 0.73-0.89 for scREFINE. Ablation analyses further demonstrate that task-specific embedding refinement is the primary driver of improvement, whereas soft structural regularization provides dataset-dependent auxiliary gains and degrades more gracefully than hard pseudo-labels when supervision is scarce. Biological marker-gene analysis confirms that the predicted clusters correspond to canonical cell populations.

records.title: Virtual metrology for process perturbation prediction in lithographic alignment marks using a physics-guided directed attention network.
records.abstract: Process perturbations in lithographic alignment marks deform multilayer profiles, break mark symmetry, and introduce alignment position uncertainty. Although alignment position deviation (APD) and wafer quality (WQ) responses contain process-dependent information, retrieving the underlying perturbations remains challenging because the inverse relationship is nonlinear and strongly coupled. We formulate this task as alignment mark virtual metrology, in which process perturbation values are estimated from paired APD/WQ response matrices. To solve this inverse problem, we propose a physics-guided directed attention network (PG-DAN). PG-DAN uses diffraction limit masked attention (DLMA) to inject wavelength, diffraction order, propagation, locality, and identity priors into APD/WQ attention logits, enabling the model to use physically meaningful token relations rather than unconstrained data correlations. A directed decoder further follows multilayer coupling during prediction. Evaluated on a rigorous coupled wave analysis (RCWA) dataset, PG-DAN achieves a mean R2 of 0.999875, a mean range-normalized RMSE of 0.34%, and a mean range-normalized MAE of 0.23%, with lower estimation errors than conventional neural inverse models. These results support physics-guided inverse modeling for alignment mark process perturbation estimation.

records.title: Single-cell perturbation prediction near experimental reproducibility with GENESIS.
records.abstract: Single-cell perturbation atlases now measure cellular responses across millions of cells, but the number of possible combinations of biological contexts, perturbations, doses and other experimental variables make exhaustive measurements infeasible. Here, we present GENESIS (Generative ENErgy-based Single-cell Intervention Simulator), a generative framework that predicts single-cell response distributions directly from the covariates defining an experimental condition. GENESIS uses a lightweight neural network trained with the energy score, a strictly proper scoring rule for distributions. We introduce an experiment-calibrated evaluation framework in which prediction error is interpreted relative to the reproducibility of repeated measurements of the same condition. Across the Tahoe-100M small-molecule atlas and a large PBMC cytokine atlas, GENESIS significantly outperforms existing generative models and statistical baselines and approaches experimental reproducibility on independently repeated conditions. Importantly, GENESIS remains accurate when trained on only a fraction of the available experimental conditions or cells, and generated profiles recover experimentally observed context-dependent transcriptional programs. At comparable training-cell budgets, GENESIS achieves more accurate predictions when measurements span more experimental conditions rather than profiling fewer conditions more deeply. Together, these findings suggest a complementary strategy for perturbation studies: broader, lower-depth measurements can expand experimental coverage, while GENESIS augments sparsely sampled populations and predicts responses in unmeasured conditions.

records.title: MultiFlow: coupled flow matching for predicting single-cell multiomic perturbation responses in unseen cellular contexts.
records.abstract: Predicting cellular responses to perturbation requires resolving coordinated changes across molecular layers, yet most single-cell perturbation models focus on transcriptional responses alone. Here we present MultiFlow, a coupled flow-matching framework that unifies generation and perturbation prediction of paired gene expression and chromatin accessibility. Through bidirectional information exchange between RNA and ATAC generative flows, MultiFlow learns how their joint distribution depends on cellular context and perturbation identity. Across multiomic generation benchmarks, MultiFlow accurately reproduced paired RNA-ATAC states and their population distributions. In multiome perturbation benchmarks, MultiFlow achieved the strongest overall performance in predicting both gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility perturbation responses, outperforming modality-specific perturbation-prediction methods in cell types whose perturbed states were withheld from training. Joint multiomic modeling further preserved perturbation-induced coordination between modalities, including concordant peak-gene effects and cross-modal cellular neighborhood structure. These results establish MultiFlow as a unified generative framework for modeling paired molecular states and predicting their coordinated perturbation responses across cellular contexts. Code and tutorial of MultiFlow are available at https://github.com/liuq-lab/MultiFlow.

records.title: Prediction transfer does not imply reliability transfer in single-cell foundation models.
records.abstract: Single-cell foundation models are increasingly transferred across tissues, diseases, perturbation screens, and experimental platforms. Although substantial effort has focused on prediction transfer, it remains unclear whether a model's assessment of its own reliability transfers similarly across biological contexts. Here we define reliability transfer as the ability to transfer an accurate assessment of when model predictions are likely to be correct or incorrect and investigate its behavior across ten perturbation-prediction systems spanning multiple datasets, models, and evaluation settings. We find that reliability transfer varies substantially across source-target pairs and cannot be inferred from predictive performance alone, indicating that prediction transfer and reliability transfer constitute distinct forms of generalization. Analyses of biological annotations, network connectivity, target exposure, and contextual factors reveal that prediction reliability is associated with both shared and context-dependent signals, with their relative importance differing across systems. To characterize this variability, we introduce reliability-attribution fingerprints, context-level signatures derived from strictly cross-fitted SHAP explanations that summarize how reliability estimators combine biological and contextual information when assigning confidence. Across systems, contexts with similar attribution-magnitude fingerprints tended to transfer reliability more successfully, and fingerprint similarity identified transfer sources achieving higher reliability-transfer performance within the observed candidate set. However, these relationships weakened under stricter cross-family transfer settings, indicating that transferable reliability structure remains partly dependent on shared contextual information. Finally, transferred reliability estimators produced different perturbation rankings despite identical perturbation predictions, illustrating a practical consequence of reliability transfer for downstream prioritization. Together, these results establish reliability transfer as a distinct aspect of foundation-model generalization and introduce reliability-attribution fingerprints as a framework for characterizing transferable reliability structure across biological contexts.

records.title: Natural language-guided generation of molecular structures for single-molecule electronics.
records.abstract: As molecular science advances toward autonomous scientific discovery, enabling AI models to directly generate valid molecular structures from natural language descriptions has emerged as a critical requirement. While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated the ability to map discrete chemical space into continuous semantic representation for general molecular generation, their application to single-molecule electronics (SME) remains largely unexplored. This is primarily due to the specific topological requirements of the field, such as the necessity of an anchor-backbone-anchor motif for electrode connection. In this work, we propose SingMolT5, a fine-tuned molecular LLM for natural language-guided generation of single molecules. We systematically evaluated the structural generation performance using both in-context learning (ICL) and fine-tuning strategies based on a carefully curated domain-specific instruction-tuning dataset. Results show that while ICL can capture basic molecular syntax, only the fine-tuning model can reliably enforce the anchor-backbone-anchor motif required for single-molecule measurements. More importantly, SingMolT5 achieved high structural prediction accuracy, along with strong generalization to unseen structural variations not included in the training dataset. This work provides a proof-of-concept demonstration for a text-to-structure workflow in SME, serving as a foundational step toward integrating natural language models into future autonomous workflows for single-molecule research.

records.title: Rapid assessment of chemical complementarity of ligands for protein design.
records.abstract: Driven by deep-learning methods, computational protein design can now rapidly generate de novo structures, opening new frontiers for creating proteins that bind small molecules tightly and specifically, although achieving predictable and tunable binding remains challenging. Here we address this with a rapid physics-based computational method to generate isosteric and chemically complementary binding pockets for small-molecule targets in de novo designed proteins. We test this experimentally by constructing and characterizing binding proteins for several synthetic and natural chromophores. By evaluating only single-digit numbers of designs, the pipeline delivers stable proteins with pre-organised binding sites in apo structures confirmed by X-ray crystallography, which bind the targets with micromolar affinities or better. To illustrate the scope and applications of this approach, we incorporate selective and coupled chromophore-binding sites in a two-domain de novo protein enabling controlled energy transfer between the two sites, and we develop a small de novo binding protein that can be used in live mammalian cells to visualise sub-cellular structures.

records.title: Genetically encoded chemically controlled proximity switches: Molecular design, pharmacology, and therapeutic considerations.
records.abstract: Genetically encoded chemically controlled proximity systems are chemogenetic tools that utilize small molecules to regulate protein association, higher-order assembly, and dissociation. Over the past three decades, an expanding repertoire of these systems has transformed the study of protein function and cellular signaling by enabling rapid, reversible, and tunable manipulation of protein localization, assembly, activity, and downstream physiological processes. As these technologies advance from experimental tools toward therapeutic applications, their translational potential depends not only on molecular switch performance but also on the properties of the chemical inducer and engineered protein components. In this review, we summarize the major classes and design principles of representative genetically encoded chemically controlled proximity systems, with particular emphasis on the pharmacological determinants that define their therapeutic operating window, including pharmacodynamic orthogonality, pharmacokinetics, tissue exposure, endogenous target engagement, and clinical readiness. We also examine how the biological origin and engineering of the chemogenetic modules influence immunogenicity and long-term compatibility. We further discuss exemplary applications, including pharmacological control of CAR-T cell activity, programmed cell death, CRISPR-based genome and epigenome engineering, and on-demand secretion of therapeutic proteins. Finally, we consider the delivery and coordinated expression of chemically regulated protein components as major remaining barriers to therapeutic implementation and highlight clinically compatible inducers, compact and minimally immunogenic protein modules, de novo protein design, and advances in viral and nonviral delivery as promising directions toward more reliable and pharmacologically tractable chemically controlled therapies.

records.title: Chemical Biology in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: From Ligand Discovery to Virtual Cells.
records.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing how scientists, including chemical biologists, conduct research. This review is intended to serve as an introduction for chemical biologists to applications of artificial intelligence in chemical biology. We review how chemical and biological data are featurized, the types of models commonly used in chemical biology applications, challenges in assessing accuracy of artificial intelligence models, and recent developments in agentic artificial intelligence for autonomous research. The applications we will cover include protein structure prediction, ligand discovery, peptide and protein design, prediction of mutational effects, interactomics and gene regulation, and virtual cells.

records.title: An AI-designed, recombinantly produced FtsZ-directed peptide with in vitro activity against pan-drug-resistant clinical isolates.
records.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is outpacing the antibiotic pipeline, yet antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) - the most-cited alternative class - remain constrained by proteolytic instability, host toxicity, and the cost of solid-phase synthesis. We report an integrated design-to-validation pipeline that addresses these constraints and yields a de novo peptide directed at an intracellular, non-lytic target. Instead of relying on membrane disruption, the design was directed at FtsZ, the essential bacterial cell-division GTPase, at a consensus epitope (residues 60-145) that our alignments show is substantially more conserved across the Gram-positive/Gram-negative divide than FtsZ overall (68.6% versus 50.1% identity between Enterococcus and Klebsiella orthologues) while sharing only approximately 8-24% identity with human tubulin. A sequence-space diffusion model conditioned on the amino-acid composition of experimentally validated AMPs generated ten binders; fusion to 120 cell-penetrating motifs, machine-learning triage, co-folding and replicated molecular dynamics identified a single lead, Combined111. Rather than chemical synthesis, the peptide was produced biologically: the codon-optimised gene was cloned in-house into pHT254 and expressed as an intracellular, C-terminal 8xHis-tagged product in the protease-deficient Bacillus subtilis WB800N host, giving a mean transcript induction of 3.40-fold (SD 2.01, n = 4 biological replicates) and a single band of approximately 11.1 kDa after one-step Ni-NTA purification. Against one pan-drug-resistant clinical isolate of each of seven species, the purified peptide produced larger inhibition zones than a panel of last-resort antibiotics for five of the seven, by a mean of 4.81 mm, although this difference was not statistically significant (95% CI -0.64 to 10.27; t(6) = 2.16, p = 0.074, Cohen's dz = 0.82). Each zone value is a single measurement, so reproducibility was not assessed, and inhibition-zone diameters are not a direct measure of comparative potency. The advantage was consistent in direction but not uniform, the pan-drug-resistant Enterococcus faecalis isolate being the least susceptible. E. faecium FtsZ was the sequence used for the computational design, whereas the Gram-positive organism available for experimental testing was E. faecalis. These findings show that generative design can be coupled to low-cost bacterial expression in one laboratory. FtsZ-directed inhibition is presented here as a hypothesis rather than an established mechanism: target engagement was inferred from alignment, co-folding and molecular dynamics, and no direct binding measurement, FtsZ polymerisation or GTPase assay, or Z-ring localisation experiment was performed. Minimum inhibitory concentrations, resistance selection, haemolysis, mammalian cytotoxicity, and in vivo efficacy all remain to be established.

records.title: PRIZM: combining low-N data and zero-shot models to design enhanced protein variants.
records.abstract: Machine learning has repeatedly shown the ability to accelerate protein engineering, but many approaches demand large amounts of robust, high-quality training data as well as substantial computational expertise. While large pre-trained models can function as zero-shot proxies for predicting variant effects, selecting the best model for a given protein property is often non-trivial. Here, we introduce Protein Ranking using Informed Zero-shot Modelling (PRIZM), a two-phase workflow that first uses a high-quality low-N dataset to identify the most suitable pre-trained zero-shot model for a target protein property and then applies that model to rank and prioritize an in silico variant library for experimental testing. Across diverse benchmark datasets spanning multiple protein properties, PRIZM reliably separated low- from high-performing models using datasets of ∼20 labelled variants. We further demonstrate PRIZM in enzyme engineering case studies targeting sucrose synthase thermostability and glycosyltransferase activity, where PRIZM-guided selection identified improved variants, including gains of ∼3°C in apparent melting temperature and ∼20% higher relative activity. PRIZM provides an accessible, data-efficient route to leverage foundation models for protein design while requiring minimal experimental data. PRIZM is publicly available via Zenodo, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23035983, and the PRIZM GitHub repository https://github.com/daha-la/PRIZM.

records.title: Longitudinal Detection of Circulating Tumor DNA in Children with Pleuropulmonary Blastoma: A Report from the International PPB/DICER1 Registry.
records.abstract: Pleuropulmonary blastoma (PPB) is the most common lung cancer of early childhood. Nearly all PPBs have biallelic DICER1 variants: a loss-of-function allele (often germline) and a second RNase IIIb domain "hotspot" substitution. Except in somatic mosaicism, these hotspots are tumor-specific and ideal liquid biopsy targets. For individuals with PPB enrolled in the International PPB/DICER1 Registry, blood samples were collected at timepoints coordinated with clinical venous access. Tumor sequencing identified each patient's RNase IIIb hotspot, enabling personalized droplet digital PCR assays to detect that variant in circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA). We analyzed 482 samples from 20 type I and 53 type II/III PPB patients. Among 13 pre-operative type II/III patients sampled pretreatment, 11 (85%) had detectable ctDNA, with tumor size moderately correlated with ctDNA burden (Spearman's ρ=0.574, p=0.051). In contrast, among 8 patients sampled after resection but before chemotherapy, none had detectable ctDNA (p<0.001 vs. unresected). After chemotherapy initiation, ctDNA levels spiked within 1-2 days before rapidly declining. During post-event surveillance, ctDNA was detectable a median of 5.3 weeks before clinical progression (21.7 weeks for negative samples; p=0.001). In type I PPB, DICER1 variants were detectable only in patients with somatic mosaicism. In type II/III PPB, ctDNA correlates with tumor size and resection status. The transient rise and fall in ctDNA following initiation of chemotherapy suggests that ctDNA could serve as a real-time in vivo assay of tumor responsiveness, and these findings support further investigation as a pharmacodynamic biomarker for disease response and recurrence detection.

records.title: Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 Testing and Clinical Decision-Making in Gastroesophageal Adenocarcinoma: Guideline Update From the College of American Pathologists in Collaboration With the American Society for Clinical Pathology.
records.abstract: With advances in treatment options and clinical trials for patients with advanced gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma (GEA), human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2, ERBB2 [erb-b2 receptor tyrosine kinase 2]) testing in GEA continues to evolve. To assess evidence published since the 2016 College of American Pathologists (CAP)/American Society for Clinical Pathology (ASCP)/American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) HER2 testing in GEA guideline and to update evidence-based recommendations. The CAP convened a panel of experts to update the guideline, following standards established by the National Academy of Medicine for developing trustworthy clinical practice guidelines. The expert panel defined key questions and performed a systematic review of the literature. Using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach, recommendations were updated based on available evidence, certainty of evidence, and key judgments. Three strong recommendations were developed. Of 6 statements from the 2016 CAP-ASCP-ASCO guideline released for public comment, 4 were reaffirmed as good practice statements for the assessment of HER2 in advanced GEA, and 2 were archived. The expert panel recommends that at initial diagnosis of advanced GEA, testing should be performed on the highest-quality tumor specimen. Immunohistochemistry followed by in situ hybridization, if indicated, should be used as the primary assessment for HER2 status. Genomic testing may be used concurrently or subsequently for clinical decision-making. In patients considered for subsequent therapy after disease progression, testing may be performed on relapsed/recurrent tumor. Tissue is preferable but testing may be performed on liquid biopsy.

records.title: Plasma Extracellular Vesicles as Biomarkers of Coronary Artery Disease: A Proteomic Analysis Using DIA-MS-Based Proteomics.
records.abstract: Coronary artery disease (CAD) remains one of the leading causes of death worldwide, highlighting the need for improved molecular tools to monitor disease progression and cardiac function. Extracellular vesicles (EVs), released by most cell types into the bloodstream, encapsulate bioactive proteins and can serve as a sensitive matrix for proteomic analysis. The aim of this study was to compare the proteomic profiles of plasma and plasma-derived EVs using data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry (DIA-MS) and to evaluate their associations with clinical indicators of heart failure risk. We analyzed plasma and EVs from 28 individuals, including patients undergoing routine clinical follow-up to assess heart disease risk and patients diagnosed with CAD. EV-derived proteome demonstrated stronger and/or more numerous correlations with key clinical parameters of cardiac function and stress, namely Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), and Troponin I (TnI), than the neat plasma proteome. These findings underscore the potential of EVs to sensitively reflect dynamic and localized molecular alterations associated with myocardial injury and dysfunction. In contrast, neat plasma proteomes were more closely associated with structural cardiac parameters, such as increased left ventricular mass. Taken together, these results suggest that while both matrices offer complementary insights, EVs may provide a more refined and functionally relevant view of ongoing cardiovascular pathology, particularly in the context of coronary disease-induced myocardial stress. Plasma-derived EVs represent a biologically informative compartment that offers a more sensitive and direct window to the heart status than plasma proteomics. The stronger association of plasma-derived EVs with clinically relevant variables supports the value of integrating EV-based proteomics into cardiovascular research.

records.title: The dual role of small EVs in asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: from pathogenesis to clinical translation.
records.abstract: Asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) are leading causes of chronic respiratory morbidity, yet current therapies fail to halt airway remodeling or disease progression. Small extracellular vesicles (small EVs), a nanoscale subset of extracellular vesicles that includes exosomes, have emerged as key mediators of intercellular communication in the lung, transferring proteins, lipids and nucleic acids to modulate inflammation, immunity and tissue repair. Their cargo reflects donor cell state and can be sampled from biofluids, suggesting their potential as liquid-biopsy biomarkers and therapeutic vehicles. Notably, small EVs exert context-dependent bidirectional effects in asthma and COPD, either exacerbating airway inflammation and remodeling or suppressing immune responses and promoting repair. This review synthesizes the biological functions of small EVs in these diseases, dissects mechanisms underlying their dual roles, and evaluates their translational potential as biomarkers and candidate therapeutic strategies, while outlining critical challenges in isolation, standardization and clinical validation.

records.title: Spatiotemporal remodeling of the tumor-immune interface during neoadjuvant immunotherapy for oral squamous cell carcinoma: pathological response, resistance, and dynamic biomarkers.
records.abstract: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is locally aggressive and frequently associated with cervical lymph-node metastasis and postoperative recurrence. Recent clinical advances in perioperative immunotherapy have made the neoadjuvant setting an important window for investigating dynamic changes in the tumor-immune microenvironment under therapeutic pressure. However, pathological responses vary substantially among patients, and baseline biomarkers such as the PD-L1 combined positive score (CPS) and tumor mutational burden (TMB) do not reliably identify those most likely to benefit. Evidence from single-cell sequencing, spatial omics, multiplex imaging, and longitudinal liquid-biopsy studies indicates that pathological response is closely associated with antigen presentation, expansion-competent T cells, tertiary lymphoid structures, vascular routes of immune-cell entry, and myeloid-stromal remodeling. In contrast, impaired antigen presentation, T-cell exclusion, immunosuppressive macrophages, cancer-associated fibroblasts, hypoxic metabolism, and lymph-node-specific niches are associated with residual resistance. This review examines spatiotemporal changes at the tumor-immune interface before and after neoadjuvant immunotherapy for OSCC, with an emphasis on pathological response, mechanisms of resistance, and dynamic biomarkers. We also discuss the translational potential of these features for patient stratification and perioperative treatment decision-making.

records.title: Multiomic liquid biopsy: emerging applications in disease quantification, biomarker detection, molecular phenotyping, and cancer signal of origin prediction.
records.abstract: The field of cancer-related liquid biopsy, largely defined as plasma circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) analysis by next-generation sequencing (NGS), is rapidly evolving from genomics-only approaches to multiomic assays that add components such as DNA fragmentomics and epigenomics, with or without proteomics, to a genomic backbone. Here we describe how integration of epigenomic profiling, particularly tumor-specific methylation signatures, may extend ctDNA testing beyond detection of genomic alterations toward broader molecular phenotyping, with applications in alternative approaches to tumor fraction quantification, enhanced detection of actionable genomic biomarkers and mechanisms of resistance, histologic and lineage characterization, and cancer signal of origin prediction. This evolution has facilitated the clinical application of liquid biopsy across the cancer care continuum, from screening/early detection to determining minimal residual disease (MRD) in early-stage cancers to selecting treatment and determining mechanisms of acquired resistance in advanced-stage cancers. These new multiomic assays may also support prospective biomarker-driven clinical trials incorporating complementary measures of tumor burden, genomic alterations, and molecular phenotype. Collectively, these advances suggest that multiomic liquid biopsy platforms may represent a major advance in precision oncology, enabling dynamic and comprehensive characterization of tumor biology.
